{{Cosmology|scientists}}

'''George Fitzgerald Smoot III''' (February 20, 1945 – September 18, 2025) was an American [[astrophysicist]] and [[cosmologist]]. He shared the 2006 [[Nobel Prize in Physics]] with [[John C. Mather]] "for their discovery of the [[black body]] form and [[anisotropy]] of the [[cosmic microwave background radiation]]".<ref>{{cite web| title=The Nobel Prize in Physics 2006| work=The Nobel Foundation| url=https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/2006/summary/}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=All Nobel Prizes in Physics |url=https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/lists/all-nobel-prizes-in-physics/ |access-date=October 21, 2025 |website=The Nobel Prize}}</ref>

This work helped further the [[Big Bang]] theory of the universe using the [[Cosmic Background Explorer]].<ref>{{cite news| last= Horgan| first= John| author-link=John Horgan (journalist)| year= 1992| title= Profile: George F. Smoot – COBE's Cosmic Cartographer| journal= [[Scientific American]] |volume= 267| number= 1| pages= 34–41 | doi= 10.1038/scientificamerican0792-34 }}</ref> According to the Nobel Prize committee, "the COBE project can also be regarded as the starting point for [[cosmology]] as a precision science."<ref>{{cite press release |url=http://nobelprize.org/nobel_prizes/physics/laureates/2006/info.html |title=The Nobel Prize in Physics 2006 |publisher=The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences |format=PDF |date=October 3, 2006 |access-date=October 5, 2006 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100815040431/http://nobelprize.org/nobel_prizes/physics/laureates/2006/info.html |archive-date=August 15, 2010 }}</ref> In 2007, Smoot donated $500,000 to fund the Berkeley Center for Cosmological Physics,<ref name= Berk-obit>{{cite news| title= Nobelist George Smoot, whose satellite experiments validated the Big Bang theory, dies at 80 |url= https://news.berkeley.edu/2025/09/29/nobelist-george-smoot-whose-satellite-experiments-validated-the-big-bang-theory-dies-at-80/| first= Robert| last= Sanders| website= berkeley.edu| publisher= University of California Berkeley | access-date= 2025-09-30}}</ref> and an additional amount from his Nobel Prize money, less travel costs, to the East Bay
Community Foundation, a charity.<ref>{{cite news | url= http://ebcf.org/press/07/Smoot_AP_3-07.pdf | title=Berkeley Nobel laureates donate prize money to charity | agency=[[Associated Press]] | date=March 22, 2007 | access-date=March 31, 2010 | archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20110726012539/http://www.ebcf.org/press/07/Smoot_AP_3-07.pdf | archive-date=July 26, 2011 }}</ref> 

Smoot had been at the [[University of California, Berkeley]], and the [[Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory]] since 1970. He was Chair of the Endowment Fund "Physics of the Universe" of Paris Center for Cosmological Physics. Apart from being elected a member of the US [[National Academy of Sciences]] and a Fellow of the [[American Physical Society]], Smoot had been honored by several universities worldwide with doctorates or professorships. He was also the recipient of the [[Gruber Prize in Cosmology]] (2006), the Daniel Chalonge Medal from the [[International School of Astrophysics]] (2006), the [[Einstein Medal]] from the [[Albert Einstein Society]] (2003), the [[Ernest Orlando Lawrence Award]] from the [[U.S. Department of Energy]] (1995), and the [[Exceptional Scientific Achievement Medal]] from NASA (1991). He was a member of the advisory board of the journal ''[[Universe (journal)|Universe]]''.<ref>{{citation |url=https://www.mdpi.com/journal/universe/editors?search=smoot |title=Editorial Board – Members |publisher= | website= MDPI.com |access-date=September 25, 2025}}</ref>

Smoot was one of the 20 American recipients of the Nobel Prize in Physics to sign a letter addressed to President [[George W. Bush]] in May 2008, urging him to "reverse the damage done to [[basic science research]] in the Fiscal Year 2008 Omnibus Appropriations Bill" by requesting additional emergency funding for the Department of Energy's [[Office of Science]], the [[National Science Foundation]], and the [[National Institute of Standards and Technology]].<ref>{{cite web|title=A Letter from America's Physics Nobel Laureates|url=https://fire.pppl.gov/nobel_bush_fy08_050808.pdf| website= pppl.gov| publisher= [[Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory]] | date= | access-date= 2025-09-30}}</ref>

==Early life, family and education==
Smoot was born in [[Yukon, Florida]], on February 20, 1945.<ref name=lemonde/><ref name=LBNL>{{cite web|title=George F. Smoot III |publisher= Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory|url=https://www.lbl.gov/people/excellence/nobelists/george-f-smoot-iii/|work= lbl.gov |access-date=September 28, 2025}}</ref> His father was a hydrologist for the [[US Geological Survey]], and his mother was a teacher and school principal.<ref name= Berk-obit /><ref name="lemonde">{{Cite news |last=Barthélémy |first=Pierre |date= September 25, 2025 |title=George Smoot, explorateur de la soupe cosmique primordiale et Prix Nobel de physique, est mort |url= https://www.lemonde.fr/disparitions/article/2025/09/25/george-smoot-explorateur-de-la-soupe-cosmique-primordiale-et-nobel-de-physique-est-mort_6642966_3382.html |work=[[Le Monde]] |language=fr| trans-title= George Smoot, explorer of the primordial cosmic soup and Nobel Prize winner in physics, has died| url-status= live| archiveurl= https://archive.today/20250925223226/https://www.lemonde.fr/disparitions/article/2025/09/25/george-smoot-explorateur-de-la-soupe-cosmique-primordiale-et-nobel-de-physique-est-mort_6642966_3382.html| archivedate= 2025-09-25 |url-access= |access-date=September 30, 2025}}</ref> He had a sister, Sharon.<ref name= Berk-obit /> Their maternal grandfather was [[Johnson T. Crawford|Johnson Tal Crawford]]. The family lived in [[Alaska]] before relocating to Ohio.<ref name="lemonde" /><ref name= Berk-obit /> He graduated from [[Upper Arlington High School (Ohio)|Upper Arlington High School]] in [[Upper Arlington, Ohio]], in 1962.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Jones|first1=Gregory L.|title=Nobel Prize winner returns home| url= http://aether.lbl.gov/PDFs/UANewsGeorgeSmoot041807.pdf| work= [[Upper Arlington News]] |date=April 18, 2007| via= lbl.gov |url-status= dead| archiveurl= https://web.archive.org/web/20200807084122/http://aether.lbl.gov/PDFs/UANewsGeorgeSmoot041807.pdf| archivedate= 2020-08-07 |access-date= 2025-09-30}}</ref> 

At the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]], he obtained dual bachelor's degrees in mathematics and physics in 1966, then a PhD in [[particle physics]] in 1970.<ref name=LBNL/><ref name="thesis-smoot-1971">{{cite thesis |url=https://www.proquest.com/docview/302620738 |title=Charge exchange of positive Kaon on platinum at three GeV/C |date=1971 |publisher=[[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] |degree=Ph.D. |last=Smoot |first= George Fitzgerald III |id={{ProQuest|302620738}} |url-access=subscription |oclc=25256702}}</ref><ref>{{cite press release | title=Nobelists' work supports big-bang theory | publisher= Massachusetts Institute of Technology | date=October 3, 2006 | url=http://web.mit.edu/newsoffice/2006/smoot.html | access-date=October 3, 2006}}</ref> A distant relative, [[Oliver R. Smoot]], was the MIT student who was used as the unit of measure known as the [[smoot]].<ref>{{cite web |url=https://archive.boston.com/news/nation/articles/2006/10/04/at_mit_future_nobelist_not_above_a_prank_or_two/ |title=At MIT, future Nobelist not above a prank or two |newspaper=[[The Boston Globe]] |date=October 4, 2006 |access-date=March 24, 2022}}</ref><ref>{{cite web| url= https://aether.lbl.gov/www/personnel/smoot/smoot-measure.html |title=The SMOOT as unit of Length |website= aether.lbl.gov| publisher= Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory| url-status= live| archiveurl= https://web.archive.org/web/20250908163035/https://aether.lbl.gov/www/personnel/smoot/smoot-measure.html| archivedate= 2025-09-08 |access-date=March 24, 2022}}</ref>

==Initial research==
Smoot switched to cosmology and began work at Berkeley, collaborating with [[Luis Walter Alvarez]] on the High Altitude Particle Physics Experiment, a [[stratosphere|stratospheric]] [[weather balloon]] designed to detect [[antimatter]] in Earth's upper atmosphere,<ref name=":0">{{Cite news |last=Corbyn |first=Zoë |date=April 19, 2014 |title=George Smoot: We mapped the embryonic universe |url=https://www.theguardian.com/science/2014/apr/20/george-smoot-we-mapped-embryonic-universe-nobel-winning-big-bang-cosmos |access-date=September 25, 2025 |work=The Guardian |language=en-GB |issn=0261-3077}}</ref> the presence of which was predicted by the now discredited [[steady state theory]] of cosmology.

He then took up an interest in [[cosmic microwave background radiation]] (CMB), previously discovered by [[Arno Allan Penzias]] and [[Robert Woodrow Wilson]] in 1964. There were, at that time, several open questions about this topic, relating directly to fundamental questions about the structure of the [[universe]]. Certain models predicted the universe as a whole was rotating, which would have an effect on the CMB: its temperature would depend on the direction of observation. With the help of Alvarez and [[Richard A. Muller]], Smoot developed a differential [[radiometer]] which measured the difference in temperature of the CMB between two directions 60 degrees apart. The instrument, which was mounted on a [[Lockheed U-2]] plane, made it possible to determine that the overall rotation of the universe was zero, which was within the limits of accuracy of the instrument. It did, however, detect a variation in the temperature of the CMB of a different sort. That the CMB appears to be at a higher temperature on one side of the sky than on the opposite side, referred to as a dipole pattern, has been explained as a [[Doppler effect]] of the Earth's motion relative to the area of CMB emission, which is called the [[last scattering surface]]. Such a Doppler effect arises because the Sun, and in fact the [[Milky Way]] as a whole, is not stationary, but rather is moving at nearly 600&nbsp;km/s with respect to the last scattering surface. This is probably due to the [[gravity|gravitational attraction]] between our galaxy and a concentration of mass like the [[Great Attractor]].<ref name=":0" />

==Cosmic Background Explorer (COBE)==
[[File:COBE cmb fluctuations.png|thumb|300px|left|Map of the CMB fluctuations found by COBE.]]

At that time, the CMB appeared to be perfectly uniform excluding the distortion caused by the Doppler effect as mentioned above. This result contradicted observations of the universe, with various structures such as [[galaxy|galaxies]] and [[galaxy cluster]]s indicating that the universe was relatively [[heterogeneous]] on a small scale. However, these structures formed slowly. Thus, if the universe is heterogeneous today, it would have been heterogeneous at the time of the emission of the CMB as well, and observable today through weak variations in the temperature of the CMB. It was the detection of these anisotropies that Smoot was working on in the late 1970s. He then proposed to [[NASA]] a project involving a [[satellite]] equipped with a detector that was similar to the one mounted on the U-2 but was more sensitive and not influenced by air pollution. The proposal was accepted and incorporated as one of the instruments of the satellite [[Cosmic Background Explorer]] (COBE), which cost $160 million. COBE was launched on November 18, 1989, after a delay owing to the destruction of the [[Space Shuttle Challenger]]. After more than two years of observation and analysis, the COBE research team announced on April 23, 1992, that the satellite had detected tiny fluctuations in the CMB, a breakthrough in the study of the early universe.<ref>{{cite journal | last=Smoot | first=G.F. |display-authors=etal |date=September 1992 | title=Structure in the COBE differential microwave radiometer first-year maps | journal=Astrophysical Journal | volume=396 | issue=1 | pages=L1–L5 | doi=10.1086/186504 | bibcode=1992ApJ...396L...1S| s2cid=120701913 | doi-access=free }}</ref> The observations were "evidence for the birth of the universe" and led Smoot to say regarding the importance of his discovery that "if you're religious, it's like looking at God."<ref>{{cite news | agency=Associated Press | title=U.S. Scientists Find a 'Holy Grail': Ripples at Edge of the Universe | page=1 | work=[[International Herald Tribune]] | date=April 24, 1992}}</ref><ref>{{cite news | first=Thomas H. II| last= Maugh | title=Relics of Big Bang, Seen for First Time | pages=A1, A30 | work=[[Los Angeles Times]] | date=April 24, 1992}}</ref>

[[File:George Smoot.jpg|left|thumb|Smoot celebrating his Nobel Prize at [[Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory]], October 3, 2006]]

The success of COBE was the outcome of extensive teamwork involving more than 1,000 researchers, engineers and other participants. John Mather coordinated the entire process and also had primary responsibility for the experiment that revealed the blackbody form of the CMB measured by COBE. Smoot had the main responsibility of measuring the small variations in the temperature of the radiation.<ref>{{cite press release | title=Pictures of a Newborn Universe | url=http://nobelprize.org/nobel_prizes/physics/laureates/2006/press.html | publisher=Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences | date=October 3, 2006 | access-date=September 5, 2007}}</ref>

Smoot collaborated with ''[[San Francisco Chronicle]]'' journalist Keay Davidson to write the general-audience book ''[[Wrinkles in Time]]'', that chronicled his team's efforts.<ref>{{cite book | last=Smoot | first=George | author2=Davidson, Keay | title=Wrinkles in Time | location=New York | publisher= W. Morrow | date=1993 | isbn=0-688-12330-9 | url=https://archive.org/details/wrinklesintime00geor }}</ref> In the book ''The Very First Light'', John Mather and John Boslough complemented and broadened the COBE story,<ref>{{cite book | last=Mather | first=John | author2=Boslough, John | title=The Very First Light: The True Inside Story of the Scientific Journey Back to the Dawn of the Universe | location=New York | publisher=[[Basic Books]] | date=1997 | isbn=0-465-01575-1 | url=https://archive.org/details/veryfirstlight00john }}</ref> but also suggested that Smoot violated team policy by leaking news of COBE's discoveries to the press before NASA's formal announcement, a leak that, to Mather, smacked of self-promotion and betrayal. Smoot eventually apologized for not following the agreed publicity plan and Mather said tensions eventually eased. Mather acknowledged that Smoot had "brought COBE worldwide publicity" the project might not normally have received.<ref>{{cite news | first= Lynn| last= Yarris | title=After the Phone Call | url=http://www.lbl.gov/Science-Articles/Archive/sabl/2006/Oct/4.html | work=Science@Berkeley Lab | date=October 26, 2006| publisher= Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory | access-date=September 5, 2007 | archive-date=May 6, 2008 | archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20080506003000/http://www.lbl.gov/Science-Articles/Archive/sabl/2006/Oct/4.html }}</ref>

==Other projects==
After COBE, Smoot took part in another experiment involving a stratospheric balloon, [[Millimeter Anisotropy eXperiment IMaging Array]], which had improved angular resolution compared to COBE, and refined the measurements of the anisotropies of the CMB. Smoot has continued CMB observations and analysis and was a collaborator on the third generation CMB anisotropy observatory [[Planck satellite]]. He was also a collaborator of the design of the [[Supernova/Acceleration Probe]], a satellite which is proposed to measure the properties of [[dark energy]].<ref>{{cite web | title=Supernova/Acceleration Probe (SNAP) | url=http://snap.lbl.gov | website= snap.lbl.gov | publisher= Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory | access-date=September 5, 2007}}</ref> He has also assisted in analyzing data from the [[Spitzer Space Telescope]] in connection with measuring [[Infrared astronomy|far infrared background radiation]].<ref>{{cite web | title=Spitzer Cosmic Far-IR Background Project | url=http://www-astro.lbl.gov/~bruce/spitzerlblpage | website= lbl.gov| publisher=Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory | access-date=September 5, 2007}}</ref>

Smoot was credited by [[Mickey Hart]] with inspiring the album ''[[Mysterium Tremendum]]'', which is based, in part on "sounds" that can be extracted from the background signature of the Big Bang.<ref>{{cite web|title = Into the Heart of Music: Recording the Mickey Hart Band's 'Mysterium Tremendum'| publisher= Grateful Dead|url = http://www.dead.net/features/blair-jackson/heart-music-recording-mickey-hart-band-s-mysterium-tremendum|website = dead.net| date=April 16, 2012 |access-date = January 2, 2016}}</ref>

Smoot was an [[artificial intelligence]] scientist for the [[GTA Foundation]], whose business is storing [[genomic sequencing]] data and using it in scientific applications.

Smoot joined [[Kazakhstan]]'s National Council for Science and Technology in January 2023.<ref>{{Cite web |url= https://www.inform.kz/ru/kasym-zhomart-tokaev-podpisal-ukaz-o-sozdanii-nacsoveta-po-nauke-i-tehnologiyam-pri-prezidente-rk_a4028235|title= Касым-Жомарт Токаев подписал указ о создании Нацсовета по науке и технологиям при Президенте РК| trans-title= Kassym-Jomart Tokayev signed a decree establishing the National Council for Science and Technology under the President of the Republic of Kazakhstan| language= ru |website= inform.kz|date=January 26, 2023 | access-date= }}</ref>

==Media appearances==
Smoot had a [[cameo appearance]] as himself in "[[The Terminator Decoupling]]" episode of ''[[The Big Bang Theory]]''.<ref>{{Cite episode | title = The Terminator Decoupling | episode-link = The Terminator Decoupling | series = [[The Big Bang Theory]] | network = CBS | date = March 9, 2009 | season = 2 | number = 17 | minutes = 20}}</ref> He contacted the show as a fan of their often physics-based plots and was incorporated into an episode featuring him lecturing at a fictional physics symposium.<ref>{{cite web | title=The Big Bang Theory Videos | url=http://www.cbs.com/shows/big_bang_theory/video/ | publisher=CBS | access-date=August 4, 2012}}</ref> He is also credited by the producer of the show with providing a joke told by Penny in the episode "[[The Dead Hooker Juxtaposition]]".<ref>{{cite web|last=Lorre|first=Chuck|title=Big Bang Theory Season 2 Episode 19 Vanity Card| url= http://www.chucklorre.com/index-bbt.php?p=247|access-date=January 17, 2014}}</ref> He appeared in a later episode, "[[The Laureate Accumulation]]", initially broadcast in April 2019.

On September 18, 2009, Smoot appeared on an episode of the [[Fox Broadcasting Company|Fox]] television show ''[[Are You Smarter Than a 5th Grader?]]'' During filming, he reached the final question, "What US state is home to [[Acadia National Park]]?", to which he gave the correct answer "[[Maine]]", becoming the second person to win a million-dollar prize.<ref name= Berk-obit /><ref>{{cite web|title=Are You Smarter Than 5th Grader? Season 3 Ep. 27 |url= http://www.hulu.com/watch/96145/are-you-smarter-than-a-5th-grader-episode-27 |publisher=FOX, Mark Burnett Productions |access-date=September 26, 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090922222702/http://www.hulu.com/watch/96145/are-you-smarter-than-a-5th-grader-episode-27 |archive-date= September 22, 2009 }}</ref>

On December 10, 2009, he appeared in a [[BBC]] interview of Nobel laureates, discussing the value science has to offer society.

Smoot gave a 2014 [[TEDx]] lecture in which he suggested that certain aspects of physics support the [[simulation hypothesis]], the idea that our reality is a computer-generated [[virtual reality]].<ref name="tedx">{{cite web|url=https://tedxtalks.ted.com/video/You-are-a-simulation-physics-ca;Recent |title=You are a Simulation & Physics Can Prove It: George Smoot at TEDxSalford|website=Tedx Talks|date=February 11, 2014}}</ref><ref name="express">{{cite web|url=http://www.express.co.uk/news/science/647161/Humans-already-living-in-a-COMPUTER-SIMULATION-leading-Nobel-Prize-astrophysicist-warns|title=Humans already living in a Computer Simulation, leading Nobel Prize astrophysicist warns|author=Sean Martin|website=Express.co.uk|date=February 24, 2016}}</ref>

In 2016, Smoot appeared in a television commercial for [[Intuit]] [[TurboTax]], advising a user of the software on what to do.<ref>Staff. (January 4, 2016) [http://www.adweek.com/adfreak/physics-geniuses-illustrate-mind-bending-simplicity-turbotax-wks-new-ads-168817 "Physics Geniuses Illustrate the Mind-Bending Simplicity of TurboTax in W+K's New Ads; Campaign will include a Super Bowl spot By David Gianatasio"] ''[[Adweek]]''</ref>

==Personal life and death==
Smoot died from a heart attack in Paris, on September 18, 2025, at age 80.<ref name="lemonde" /> The [[Astroparticle and Cosmology Laboratory]] announced his death on September 25.<ref>{{cite web |title=In Memory – George Fitzgerald Smoot, III |url= https://apc.u-paris.fr/fr/memory-george-fitzgerald-smoot-iii |website= AstroParticule & Cosmologie |access-date=September 25, 2025}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | title=Nobel laureate George Smoot, who researched the universe's origins at UC Berkeley, dies at 80 | website=[[Associated Press News]] | date=September 30, 2025 | url=https://apnews.com/article/physicist-george-smooth-big-bang-nobel-berkeley-3e4f1ac718c627806bcfd7c4653c5b54 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web | last=Miller | first=Katrina | title=George F. Smoot, Who Showed How the Cosmos Began, Is Dead at 80 | website=The New York Times | date=2025-10-20 | url=https://www.nytimes.com/2025/10/20/science/space/george-f-smoot-dead.html | access-date=2026-02-22}}</ref>
